title: "Staircase wit" — the perfect comeback, too late
example_gloss: literally "staircase wit" — thinking of the perfect retort only after you've already left, on the stairs
bridge_note: English has no single word for this at all — it borrows the French phrase wholesale when it needs one.

title: A graveyard of silent letters
example_gloss: a lot, time, twenty — each ends in one or more letters that are simply never pronounced
bridge_note: French spelling often preserves how a word used to sound centuries ago, even after the pronunciation itself moved on — you're reading a fossil.

title: "There is" is literally "it there has"
example_gloss: There is a cat. (literally: it there has a cat)
bridge_note: English's "there is" already hides a similar oddity (why "there"?), but French makes it stranger by routing it through "avoir" (to have) instead of "to be."

title: Consonants that only exist between words
example_gloss: the friends — pronounced "lez-ami": the normally-silent -s of "les" appears only because "amis" starts with a vowel
bridge_note: The consonant is a kind of grammatical ghost — invisible on its own, audible only when summoned by the next word.

title: The specific disorientation of being somewhere foreign
example_gloss: literally "un-country-ment" — the disoriented, not-quite-yourself feeling of being outside your own country/culture
bridge_note: It's not quite homesickness and not quite culture shock — English has to describe around it, French just names it.

title: A base-20 counting system hiding inside French
bridge_note: This is a leftover from a Celtic/Norman base-20 counting system that never got fully replaced — French counts normally 1-60, then switches counting systems mid-language for 70-99.

title: Same spelling, different gender, unrelated meaning
example_gloss: the trick/turn (m) / the tower (f) — identical spelling, only the article tells them apart
bridge_note: There's no way to guess this from the word itself — gender here isn't just grammar, it's the only thing separating two completely different meanings.

title: Two words for "you," and picking wrong is a real mistake
bridge_note: Using tu with the wrong person can come across as rude or presumptuous — this isn't a style choice, it's a social rule with real stakes.

title: Vowels get swallowed before the next word, every time
example_gloss: the friend, I love, what is (le/je/que all drop their vowel before a vowel sound)
bridge_note: This isn't optional or casual — it's mandatory, baked directly into spelling. Saying "le ami" out loud would just sound wrong to a French speaker.

title: Spoken French quietly deletes half of "no"
example_gloss: I don't know. (formally: Je ne sais pas — the ne is just dropped in casual speech)
bridge_note: Textbook French keeps both negation particles; real spoken French routinely drops the first one entirely, and native speakers barely notice it's gone.
